newsitem.title: USA: U.S. and Japan resolve old music dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Japan resolve old music dispute.

text.p: The United States and Japan have resolved a dispute over American sound recordings -- from Duke Ellington to Elvis Presley -- produced between 1946 and 1971, the U.S. Trade Representative's Office said on Friday.
It has been estimated that approximately 6 million unauthorised recordings from the period are manufactured and sold annually in Japan, costing U.S. rights holders about $500 million a year.

Japan recently adopted amendments to its copyright law to protect recordings of the era, which go into effect before the end of March. Previously, only foreign recordings produced after Jan. 1, 1971, were protected under Japanese law.
The agreement was reached under the World Trade Organisation's dispute settement procedures.

"We launched this case on a clear principle to protect intellectual property rights," U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky said. "We sought -- and will now obtain -- protection for U.S. sound recordings from one of the most vibrant and popular periods in the history of American music."
The resolution was heralded by the Recording Industry Association, which thanked the trade office for its efforts.

The agreement affects some of the most beloved music ever produced by the United States including recordings by Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Johnny Cash, Patsy Cline, Bob Dylan, the Beach Boys and Otis Redding.
